subject: Cognitive Science
title: In-Group Bias
description: A quick win: understand In-Group Bias.

hook.text: Split strangers into teams by coin flip. Within minutes they prefer their own team. That fast.

buildup.text: Henri Tajfel's minimal group experiments showed that any group label—even random—triggers favoritism.

discovery.text: In-group bias makes us see our group as diverse and others as all the same. "They" become a monolith.

twist.text: It's not just preference. People allocate more resources to in-group members even at personal cost.

climax.text: Expanding the in-group—seeing shared identity—is the most reliable way to reduce prejudice.

punchline.text: We trust "us" and doubt "them" on instinct alone.

quiz.question: What triggers in-group bias?
options: Any group label, even random assignment

details.summary: In-group bias is the automatic preference for members of groups you belong to over outsiders. Even arbitrary group assignments, like shirt color, trigger favoritism in resource allocation, trust, and evaluation.
details.whyItMatters: In-group bias underlies discrimination, nationalism, and intergroup conflict. Understanding its automatic nature is essential for designing fairer institutions and policies.
takeaways: People automatically favor their own group members
Even trivially defined groups trigger the bias
It contributes to discrimination and intergroup conflict

faq.question: What is the minimal group paradigm?
faq.answer: Henri Tajfel's experiments assigned people to groups based on trivial criteria like preference for a painter. Even these meaningless groups produced favoritism: participants allocated more resources to in-group members. This proved in-group bias requires no real conflict or history.

faq.question: Can in-group bias be reduced?
faq.answer: Contact hypothesis research shows meaningful intergroup cooperation toward shared goals reduces bias. Emphasizing shared identities rather than differences also helps. Institutional safeguards like blind evaluation processes are more reliable than relying on individual attitude change.
